tagline: Tokyo's own volcanic island chain — the one place in Japan where passengers already commute by hydrofoil, on a fleet that is ageing out.
summary: The Izu Islands — Ōshima, Niijima, Shikinejima, Kōzushima and the outer chain — are Tokyo Metropolis on the open Pacific: volcanic calderas, white-sand surf beaches and onsen, all administered from the capital and reached by Tokai Kisen's jet ferries and overnight ships out of Takeshiba. This is one of the world's few living foil-borne transit markets: passengers have boarded Boeing 929-family jetfoils here for decades, so foiling is an adopted habit, not a new behaviour. The chain's geometry — a 60 nm gateway leg from Tokyo Bay, a tight 2–30 nm inter-island mesh, and 85–155 nm runs to the outer islands — maps exactly onto a modern two-platform network.

demand_signals.label: Island visitor volume
demand_signals.note: Izu + Ogasawara chains combined, predominantly the Izu Islands — a lifeline-plus-tourism flow that moves almost entirely by sea from Takeshiba Pier.
demand_signals.source: Tokyo Metropolitan Government island tourism survey, 2024

demand_signals.label: An adopted hydrofoil habit
demand_signals.value: Jetfoils in daily service since the 1980s
demand_signals.note: Tokai Kisen runs a fleet of Boeing 929-family jet ferries (Seven Island Ai, Niji, Yui) from Takeshiba to Ōshima and down the chain — Tokyo↔Ōshima in ~1h45. Passengers here already accept and pay for foil-borne travel; the question is what replaces the fleet.

demand_signals.label: Fleet-replacement window
demand_signals.value: First new jetfoil in 25 years arrived only in 2020
demand_signals.note: Seven Island Yui (2020) was Japan's first newly built jetfoil in a quarter century — the rest of the gas-turbine fleet is decades old, fuel-intensive and increasingly costly to maintain. A clean, quiet next-generation foiling fleet is the natural successor.

demand_signals.label: Weather-fragile exposed water
demand_signals.value: Sagami Bay winter swell 1.5–3.0 m; typhoons Jun–Oct
demand_signals.note: The cross-Sagami legs are notoriously rough and cancellation-prone in winter swell and typhoon season — reliability and ride comfort are the islands' biggest access pain.

use_cases.title: Next-generation island lifeline from Takeshiba
use_cases.body: Modernise an adopted habit: Tokyo's island residents and visitors already ride hydrofoils daily. A quiet, smooth, next-generation foiling shuttle on the Takeshiba ↔ Ōshima gateway (~60 nm, near the all-electric range edge) and the inter-island chain keeps the timetable the islands depend on — with a dramatically better ride.

use_cases.title: Inter-island hopping mesh
use_cases.body: Ōshima ↔ Niijima ↔ Shikinejima ↔ Kōzushima sit 2–30 nm apart — a perfect all-electric mesh for surf, onsen and caldera day-trips that today require infrequent ferry connections timed around the Tokyo runs.

use_cases.title: Outer-chain line-haul
use_cases.body: Tokyo ↔ Niijima (~85 nm), Kōzushima (~95 nm) and Hachijōjima (~155 nm) exceed all-electric range — hybrid foiling line-hauls serve the outer islands with no charging-infrastructure dependency on small island grids.

use_cases.title: Cross-Sagami resort link
use_cases.body: Ōshima sits ~19–24 nm off the Izu Peninsula onsen coast (Itō/Atami) — a short foiling cross-link that stitches the islands into the peninsula's resort economy instead of forcing everything through Tokyo.

journeys.today: A ~1h45 ride on an ageing gas-turbine jetfoil — loud, fuel-hungry, and cancelled when Sagami Bay swell exceeds its comfort limits; the slow ship takes 6+ hours.
journeys.with_navier: A near-silent, smooth foiling shuttle flying above the swell on the same proven corridor — the natural successor to the jetfoil the islands already trust.

journeys.today: Inter-island connections are infrequent and timed around the Tokyo sailings — hopping the chain in one day is hard.
journeys.with_navier: An on-demand all-electric mesh across the 2–30 nm chain: surf at Niijima, onsen at Shikinejima, caldera at Ōshima — in a single day.

journeys.today: A short crossing on limited seasonal sailings; most visitors detour via Tokyo entirely.
journeys.with_navier: A ~20 nm foiling cross-link joining the onsen coast to the volcano island — two destination economies stitched into one network.

journeys.today: ~155 nm of open Pacific — an overnight ship or a flight; the jetfoil doesn't reach this far.
journeys.with_navier: A Quanta-LR hybrid line-haul extends the foiling network to the outer islands with no island charging infrastructure required.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The inter-island mesh (Ōshima ↔ Niijima ↔ Shikinejima ↔ Kōzushima, 2–30 nm) and the peninsula cross-links (Itō/Atami ↔ Ōshima ~19–24 nm) sit comfortably inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope. The Tokyo ↔ Ōshima gateway (~60 nm) is in range but near the range edge — flagged for a coordinate-level check before becoming a marquee routed leg.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Tokyo ↔ Niijima/Kōzushima (~85–95 nm) and the outer chain to Hachijōjima (~155 nm) are explicit hybrid line-hauls — beyond all-electric range and free of any dependency on small-island grid capacity, with foiling-through-swell stability on the exposed cross-Sagami water.

competitive_landscape: Tokai Kisen is the incumbent lifeline operator from Takeshiba: Boeing 929-family jet ferries (Seven Island Ai, Niji, Yui) plus the large ships Sarubia Maru and Tachibana Maru, with ~400k islanders and visitors moving through the network each year. That decades-deep jetfoil ridership is the strongest possible demand evidence — a market that already values flying over the water. The pain is fleet age and economics: gas-turbine jetfoils are fuel-intensive, maintenance-heavy and out of production, winter swell forces cancellations, and the outer islands fall back on slow overnight ships. The status quo proves the demand; the fleet that serves it is ageing out.

precedents.why_it_matters: Proves the phased two-platform island-network playbook — short all-electric meshes plus long hybrid line-hauls — at national scale; first 5 vessels in 2026.

precedents.what: Decades of daily jetfoil ridership on this exact corridor
precedents.why_it_matters: Foil-borne passenger travel is already an adopted habit here — next-generation foiling is a fleet upgrade, not a behaviour change.

seasonality: Typhoon season (Jun–Oct) and winter NW-wind swell (Dec–Feb) drive the cancellation calendar; Sagami Bay winter swell of 1.5–3.0 m has historically been the comfort and reliability limit for conventional fast craft. Foiling above the swell directly attacks the corridor's defining weakness, widening the operable window. Spring and autumn are calm peak-travel seasons.
regulatory_note: The Izu Islands are administered by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, with vessel certification under MLIT's Maritime Bureau and the Japan Coast Guard — a conservative but well-defined first-of-class regime, and a regulator already deeply familiar with hydrofoil passenger operations from four decades of jetfoil service. Lifeline-route status brings public service obligation funding into play, and Japan's 2050 carbon-neutrality target plus MLIT zero-emission-vessel programmes favour clean fleet renewal.
